summary: This Level 3 unit is about keeping production welding and fabrication under control while the work is being done. You will learn to plan the checks in a control plan, prove the set-up with a first-off inspection, make patrol checks of parts and settings, chart and read the results, contain and correct faults, build quality in with jigs, work instructions and change control, work out quality rates and costs, and report to management and to the welders.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It is about **monitoring the quality of production welding and fabrication**: planning the checks, carrying them out at the right times, reading the results, acting when something drifts, and reporting.

**Production welding** means making many identical or similar welded parts: brackets, grilles, trusses, frames, tank stands, trailer parts. When one setting drifts or one jig stop is knocked, every part made after that can be wrong. Good monitoring finds the drift while only a few parts are affected, instead of at final inspection when a whole batch may be spoiled.
**Who it is for:** Level 3 welders who act as team leaders, patrol inspectors or quality monitors on a production line, and supervisors who set up the checks.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the line
rows: Write a control plan from the drawing, specification, WPS and customer order: what to check, how, how often, by whom, and what to do if it fails.
Check the jig, settings and consumables, and fully inspect the first-off part before the run goes on.
Make patrol checks of parts and settings at set intervals, sample to plan, and judge welds against agreed visual standards.
Keep station logs, run charts and control charts, and work out rates, percentages and costs.
Spot trends and signals, rank fault types, and split the data by welder, machine, shift and date to find patterns.
Contain suspect parts, raise a report, find the root cause, correct it and prove the fix has worked.
Use work instructions, jigs, visual standards, mistake-proofing and change control, so faults are not made in the first place.
Share results at the line, hand over properly at shift change, and write a monthly quality report.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on first-off, patrol and last-off checks, settings, charts, sampling, faults, traceability, audits, cost of quality and reporting, with short calculations.

A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms (for example first-off, control chart, Pareto chart, containment, boundary sample, appraisal cost) and essays in full sentences, with figures worked out.

**Practical tasks** done as a group: run and monitor a short batch of welded brackets with a control plan, first-off, patrol checks, a run chart and a last-off; and analyse a month of production data and present a quality report with corrective actions.

blocks.note: Show your working in every calculation: the formula, the numbers put in, and the answer with its unit (%, mm, J$). Marks are given for the method as well as the answer.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Quality on a production line: the basics

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The written requirements for the product: drawing, standard, WPS, customer order
How far a size may vary from the drawing and still be accepted, for example a fillet leg of 6–8 mm
Meeting / not meeting a requirement. A non-conformance (NC) is any part, process or record that does not meet the specification.
Checking the product and the process: inspections, measurements, tests
The planned system that gives confidence the product will be right: procedures, qualified people, calibration, audits, records
Watching the process and the product while the work goes on, so that drift is caught early
Being able to tell, from the records, who made a part, when, with which materials, and how it was checked

blocks.h: Why final inspection alone is not enough

ul: It finds faults **late**, after cutting, welding, cleaning and perhaps painting have been added to a bad part.
It gives **no early warning**: a drifting setting can spoil a whole batch before anyone sees it.
It **misses some faults**: people checking hundreds of parts get tired, and many weld faults (lack of fusion, inside porosity) cannot be seen on the surface at all.
It checks only the product. Monitoring also checks the **process** that makes the product: settings, jig, consumables, method and people.

blocks.p: No two welds are ever exactly the same. Variation comes from six main sources, often called the **6 Ms**:

head: Source
Welding examples
rows: Training, skill, tiredness, a new welder, a changed technique
Settings drifting, worn contact tips and cables, a slipping wire feed, a worn jig stop
Tack order, weld sequence, travel speed, the work instruction followed (or not)
A new batch of wire or plate, damp electrodes, rusty or oily steel, the wrong gas
A worn or dropped gauge; two inspectors measuring a fillet in different ways
Wind on a MIG gas shield, humidity, heat, poor light, power dips

blocks.p: **Common-cause variation** is the normal small scatter of a steady process. A **special cause** is something that changes the process: a knocked stop, a new wire batch, a setting turned. Monitoring separates the two. Do not keep adjusting the process for every small normal change (this is called tampering, and it makes the spread worse); do act at once on a real signal.

blocks.note: Open-sided Jamaican sheds let breezes blow MIG gas shields away; rainy-season humidity dampens electrodes; afternoon heat wears welders out and overheats machines; power dips can upset some sets. Plan extra checks for these conditions: for example a gas-flow check when the wind picks up, and an electrode oven log in the rainy season.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Planning the monitoring: control plans and sampling

blocks.p: Before a production run starts, decide what will be checked, how, how often and by whom, and write it down. The usual document is a **control plan**. Its inputs are the drawing, the specification, the WPS, the customer's order (for example the inspection and NDT it asks for) and what went wrong on past runs.

head: Control plan column
What goes in it
rows: The production step: cutting, fit-up in the jig, tacking, welding, cleaning, final check
What is checked: a length, a gap, a weld size, the wire speed, the preheat
The size and tolerance, or the WPS range
The gauge or test: tape, square, fillet gauge, timed run-out, flowmeter, temperature crayon
How many and how often: first-off, 1 in 10, every hour, start of shift
The welder, patrol inspector, settings monitor or recorder
Where the result is written: station log, run chart, inspection sheet
What to do if the check fails, decided in advance: stop, hold parts back to the last good check, correct, record

blocks.h: A worked example: a bracket line

head: Step
Check
Method and frequency
Reaction if it fails
rows: Stop; reset the saw stop; sort the cut parts
Feeler gauge and square; first-off, then hourly
Adjust the jig; check the parts made since the last good check
Wire speed, volts, gas flow within the WPS
Timed run-out, meter, flowmeter; start of shift and every 2 hours
Reset; hold the parts welded since the last good log entry
Leg 6–8 mm; no undercut over the limit
Fillet gauge and photo board; 1 in 10
Hold; check every part back to the last good check; raise a report
Overall sizes, diagonals, clean for coating
Tape and square; last-off, plus 1 in 20

ul: Every inspection or test the customer asks for (for example 100% visual inspection plus a percentage of magnetic particle testing) is written into the control plan and the job's inspection records, so it cannot be forgotten.

An **inspection and test plan (ITP)** may set **hold points** and **witness points**. At a **hold point**, work must not go on until the named person (often the customer's inspector) has checked and released it. At a **witness point**, the customer is told and may attend, but work can continue if they do not come.

blocks.p: Checking every part (100%) is used for critical features and when a process is not yet proven. Otherwise a **sample** is checked, for example **1 part in every 10**. The plan says how much to check under normal conditions and when to change:

head: Sampling level
When
rows: The usual rate, for a steady process
After a failure, or after a change: more parts are checked until the results are good again
After a long run of good results, if the plan allows it

head: Calculation
Working
Answer
rows: How many parts are checked in a run of 360 at 1 in 15?
How many patrol checks in a 10-hour shift, one every 40 minutes?

ul: A **trial piece** (set-up piece) may be welded at the start of a shift to prove the set-up. It is often cut and etched or break-tested, and never sent out.

A **first-off** inspection is a full check of the first part made after a set-up, before the run goes on. It proves the jig, settings, materials and method can make a good part. It is repeated after any change: a new shift, a new material batch, a jig adjustment, a machine repair.
If the first-off fails, the run does **not** start. The set-up is corrected and another first-off is made and checked. The first-off is signed and kept with the records.

blocks.p: **Patrol (in-process) checks** are made at set times or intervals at each station, on sample parts **and** on the process. They show that the process is staying in control, and catch drift from wear, heat, tiredness or a new batch of material while only a few parts are affected.

The **last-off** part of the run is checked and kept for a time, labelled. It proves the process was still right at the end, so the whole run can be released. It is also a useful reference for setting up the next run of the same job.

flow: Set-up checks: jig against the drawing, settings to the WPS, consumables checked
First-off: full inspection, signed before the run goes on
Patrol checks of parts and settings at the planned intervals
If a check fails: stop, hold every part made since the last good check, correct, re-check
Last-off: checked and kept; the run is released

blocks.note: Every part should sit between two good checks. If a patrol check fails, the suspect parts are all those made since the **last good check**, including any already moved on to painting, the store or the customer.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Setting
How it is checked
Why it matters
rows: Timed run-out: feed the wire for an exact time (for example 6 seconds), measure the length and work out metres per minute
Wire speed sets the current; a slipping feed roll makes cold, undersize welds
A calibrated meter at the arc, or the set's own data logger
Dial readings drift; worn cables and bad earths lower what reaches the arc
A flowmeter on the gun nozzle
The regulator dial can read right while a leak or a kinked hose starves the nozzle
Time a measured length of weld
Changes weld size, fusion and heat input
Temperature-indicating crayons or a contact thermometer, with a sign-off on each part's record
Too cold risks cracking; too hot spoils toughness or corrosion resistance
Wire class and batch, gas type, electrodes taken from the holding oven (oven temperature logged)
The wrong or damp consumable spoils the weld metal; batch numbers give traceability

blocks.p: Some welding sets have a **data logger** (weld monitor) that records the current and voltage, and sometimes the wire speed and gas flow, of every weld. Welds made outside the set limits are flagged so they can be found and checked. A logger supports inspection; it does not replace it.

A jig makes every part the same, so a fault in the jig makes **every part wrong**. Check jigs against the drawing at set intervals and after any knock: worn or moved stops, bent locators, and spatter built up on locating faces. Record the checks.

ul: A **photo board** at each station shows acceptable and rejectable welds, so welders and inspectors judge in the same way.
A **boundary sample** (limit sample) is a marked real weld kept at the station that shows the worst appearance that may still be accepted.
With these, welders can check their own work before the inspector arrives.
Every gauge is numbered, kept in calibration, and checked before use (zero, or against a known reference).
The measuring method is agreed and written down: where on the weld, how many points, which gauge.
If two people get different readings on the same weld, check the **gauges and the method** first, before deciding who is right.
A dropped or damaged gauge is checked against a reference before it is used again. Readings taken with it since the damage are in doubt.
Before welding production parts, a welder must hold a qualification that covers the WPS (process, position, thickness), be inducted to the work instruction, and pass a trial piece on the line.
Patrol checks also watch the method: the tack order, the weld sequence, the gun angle, the PPE.
Results about people are used to help (training, coaching, better tools), not to blame.

blocks.p: Inspection finds faults; it does not prevent them. The cheapest quality comes from making it hard to do the job wrong.

head: Method
How it helps
rows: A short, illustrated sheet showing the approved method, settings, tack order, weld sequence and checks, so every welder on every shift works the same way
Locate every part in the same place with fixed stops and clamps: the same fit-up, the same size, less distortion
Photo boards and boundary samples, so welders judge their own work

Design the jig or method so an error cannot happen, or is seen at once: a pin that lets a part fit only the right way round; a counter that shows when all the welds are done; a go/no-go gauge at the station
Each tool and gauge has its place, so nothing is missing or mixed up (the 5S method: sort, set in order, shine, standardise, sustain)

blocks.p: Many quality problems start with an uncontrolled change. A new wire, gas, jig, welder, supplier, drawing revision or WPS revision is controlled like this:

flow: Write the change down and have it reviewed by the people responsible for production and quality
Check that the WPS covers it; if not, the WPS must be revised and, where needed, a new procedure qualified
Trial it, and inspect a first-off part after the change
Tighten the sampling for a time and watch the results
Record the date of the change, so any later faults can be linked to it
Update the control plan, work instruction and training records; approve in writing
If results get worse, stop the change and review it

ul: Every drawing, WPS and work instruction carries a **revision** letter or number and a date.
Only the **current revision** may be at the station. Old copies are removed (or clearly marked superseded) as soon as a new one is issued.
When a revision changes the method, the welders are briefed, and parts made to the old revision are checked.

Hot-dip galvanising dips the steel in molten zinc at about 450 °C. Closed hollow sections need the **vent and drain holes** shown on the drawing: trapped air and moisture can make a sealed section burst in the bath, and zinc cannot flow in and out to coat the inside.
Slag, spatter and weld-through coatings must be removed: the galvaniser's acid cleaning does not remove slag, and zinc will not coat over it.
**Silicone-based** anti-spatter sprays and oil-based markers are not removed by the galvaniser's cleaning and leave bare patches. Use only products the galvaniser has approved.
Check these at patrol checks, not when the parts come back from the galvaniser.

blocks.p: If frames come off the line slowly going out of square, check the jig, the tack order and the weld sequence first: those are what control shrinkage. Over-size welds add distortion as well as wasting wire and time.

blocks.h: Calculations you must be able to do

head: Measure
Formula
Worked example
rows: 9 defects in 450 m: 9 ÷ 450 = 0.02 per metre, or 2 per 100 m

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, and ask whether the answer makes sense: a pass rate can never be above 100%, and a share of faults cannot be bigger than the whole.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **run chart** plots a measurement (for example fillet leg size) in time order, with the target as a centre line and the tolerance limits drawn in. It shows at a glance whether the results are steady, drifting or jumping.

A **control chart** is a run chart with **control limits** worked out from the process itself. Collect about 20 to 25 readings from a steady process, work out the average and the normal spread (the standard deviation), and draw the limits, usually at **the average ± 3 standard deviations**. Almost every reading from an unchanged process falls inside them.

head: Example
Working
Result
rows: Leg sizes average 6.8 mm, standard deviation 0.25 mm
Lower control limit 6.05 mm; upper control limit 7.55 mm

head: Signal on the chart
What it means
rows: A point outside a control limit
Something has changed: stop, check the parts just made, find the cause
A run of about seven or more points in a row on one side of the centre line
The process has shifted, even if every point is inside the limits
About six or seven points in a row steadily rising or falling
A trend: something is wearing or drifting
A repeating pattern (for example worse every afternoon or after every shift change)
A cause linked to time, people or conditions

blocks.p: Rule sets differ slightly between charts; follow the rules in your control plan. When a signal appears, write the cause found and the action taken on the chart.

blocks.note: **Control limits** show what the process normally does. **Tolerance limits** show what the drawing allows. A reading can be inside tolerance but outside a control limit: the part is acceptable, but the process has changed and must be looked at before it produces rejects.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Compare the process spread (about 6 standard deviations wide) with the tolerance width. A simple capability index is **Cp = tolerance width ÷ process spread**.

head: Cp
What it means
rows: The spread is wider than the tolerance: some rejects are certain. Check every part (100%) until the process is improved.
It only just fits: any drift will make rejects
Room to spare, as long as the process is kept centred and monitored

blocks.p: Example: tolerance 6–8 mm (2 mm wide); standard deviation 0.25 mm, so the spread is 1.5 mm; Cp = 2 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 1.33.

A **Pareto chart** is a bar chart of fault types ranked from the most common to the least, often with a line showing the running total. Usually a few fault types cause most of the problem (the "80/20 rule"). Work on the biggest bar first.

head: If the faults are mostly ...
Look first at ...
rows: That welder's training, method and qualification (and whether he works the hardest joints)
Its settings, cables, contact tips, wire feed, gas supply and earth
Conditions on that shift: light, heat, wind, supervision, staffing, settings left by the last shift
What changed then: a new wire or plate batch, a moved jig, a new welder, a new WPS revision
The joint design, access, the jig and the work instruction for that joint

flow: **Detect**: a check fails, or a fault is reported
**Contain**: stop the station if needed; tag and quarantine every suspect part back to the last good check, including parts already moved on
**Record**: raise a non-conformance report (NCR)
**Find the root cause** from the facts: logs, charts, parts, people
**Correct**: repair or rework the parts to an approved procedure, and inspect them again
**Corrective action**: remove the cause so it cannot happen again
**Verify**: tightened sampling and the charts show the fix works
**Standardise**: update the control plan, work instruction and training; close the NCR

blocks.p: The first step after a fault is found is always **containment**: stop more bad parts moving on. Looking for the cause comes after.

An NCR records the part numbers and quantity, what was found and against which requirement, where and when, who found it, the containment taken, the cause, the decision on the parts (disposition), the corrective action and its result, and the sign-off.

head: Disposition
Meaning
rows: Made to conform by the normal process, for example a missing weld added
Made acceptable by an approved repair procedure (for example grinding out and rewelding), then inspected again to the same checks or more
Accepted although it does not conform: only with the **written approval** of the designer or customer
Bought-in material or parts that were faulty when received

blocks.note: Repaired welds must pass the same inspection again (and any NDT the specification asks for) before they move on. A repair that skips inspection is an unknown part.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Five whys**: keep asking "why?" until you reach a cause you can remove. For example:

flow: Porosity at Station 3. Why? Poor gas cover
Why? The flow at the nozzle was low
Why? The regulator had been knocked out of setting
Why? The cylinder trolley stands where the forklift turns
Why? There is no safe, marked bay for cylinders at that station: the **root cause**

blocks.p: Telling the welder to "take more care" fixes nothing here. A marked cylinder bay and a gas-flow check at the start of each shift do.

A **cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram** sets the problem at the "head" and the possible causes along "bones" for the 6 Ms (people, machine, method, material, measurement, environment). The team then checks the likely causes against the data or with a trial.
A good quality system lets **anyone who finds a serious fault** stop the work, as the system allows, and say why. Waiting for a manager while bad parts are made only adds to the cost.

ul: Parts or batches are marked with the job, the date and the welder's number or stamp.
Plate and section carry their **heat numbers**, which match the mill (material) certificates in the job file.
Wire, electrode and gas batch numbers are logged against the parts made.
Then, if a batch of wire turns out faulty, the records show exactly which parts were welded with it, and only those need checking.

head: Group
What it is
Welding examples
rows: Training welders, writing work instructions, good jigs, qualifying procedures
Patrol and final inspection, gauges and their calibration, NDT, test pieces
Grinding out and rewelding, scrap, lost time, re-inspection
Site repairs, travel, returned goods, claims, lost goodwill and future work

blocks.p: Faults cost more the later they are found: a fault caught at fit-up costs minutes; the same fault found on the customer's site costs travel, removal, site rework and reputation. That is why money spent on prevention and early checks usually saves much more in failure costs.

head: Worked example
Working
rows: A shop spends J$120 000 a month on rework and scrap. A J$90 000 jig and training plan is expected to cut that by a third.
Saving = J$120 000 ÷ 3 = J$40 000 a month. Payback = J$90 000 ÷ J$40 000 ≈ 2.3 months.

ul: A **board at the line** shows the run chart, the first-time pass rate, open problems and actions. Welders who see the results help fix problems sooner.
At **shift change**, hand over: open problems, parts on hold, settings changed and why, equipment faults, and materials running low. Write it in the handover log, not just say it.
Short toolbox talks explain a new standard, a change or a recent fault; ask the welders for their ideas: they often know the cause.

head: Audit
What it checks
rows: Finished parts, checked against the drawing and specification
That the line works to its procedures: the right WPS and work instruction at the station, checks done at the right times, records complete and honest
The whole quality system: procedures, training, calibration, document control, corrective actions (for example against ISO 9001)

ul: Fill in records **at the time** of the check, in ink or in the system, with your name, the date and the time.
Never fill in a check that was not done. A record that is false is worse than no record: the checks are unknown, so every part it covers must be treated as unchecked, and it must be reported.
Keep records for as long as the contract or the quality system says.
Output for the month, and the main measures against targets and recent months, on simple charts: first-time pass rate, repair rate, defects per metre, scrap, customer returns.
The main fault types (Pareto chart) and any patterns by station, shift or welder, presented fairly and kept private where they concern people.
The cost of rework, scrap and site repairs.
The NCRs raised, corrective actions taken and whether they worked.
Actions planned for next month, each with an owner and a date, and any decisions needed from management (for example money for a new jig).

blocks.p: Present it differently to each audience: a one-page summary of trends, costs and decisions for management; the board at the line and a short meeting for the welders, showing what is being done and thanking them for improvements.

blocks.note: Good results that last should be locked in: when a change (for example a new tack order) cuts rejects and keeps them down, write it into the work instruction and train everyone, so the gain is not lost when people change.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section.

ul: I can explain why quality is monitored during production and not only at final inspection.
I can name the six main sources of variation (6 Ms) with welding examples, and tell a normal variation from a signal.
I can write a control plan with methods, frequencies, records and reaction plans.
I can work out sample numbers and patrol frequencies, and explain normal, tightened and reduced sampling.
I can explain hold points and witness points, and make sure customer requirements reach the control plan.
I can carry out and explain first-off, patrol and last-off checks, and say which parts are suspect when a check fails.
I can check wire speed, current, voltage, gas flow, travel speed, preheat and consumables, and log them.
I can check jigs and gauges, and use photo boards and boundary samples.
I can build quality in with work instructions, jigs, mistake-proofing, change control and document control.
I can work out pass rates, reject rates, defects per metre, shares of faults and rework costs.
I can set up and read a run chart and a control chart, and act on the signals.
I can compare process spread with tolerance (capability).
I can use a Pareto chart and split data by welder, machine, shift and date.
I can contain a fault, raise an NCR, find the root cause and prove the fix.
I can explain traceability, the four groups of quality costs, and the three kinds of audit.
I can keep honest records, hand over at shift change, and write and present a monthly quality report.

terms: Appraisal cost
The cost of checking: inspection, gauges, calibration, NDT
Boundary (limit) sample
A marked weld kept at the station showing the worst appearance still accepted
Change control
Reviewing, trialling, approving and recording any change before it is used in production
Common cause / special cause
Normal small scatter of a steady process / a change that shifts the process
Concession
Written approval from the designer or customer to use a non-conforming part as it is
Containment
The first action after a fault: holding and checking suspect parts so no more bad parts move on
Control chart
A chart of a measurement in time order, with a centre line and control limits worked out from the process
Control plan
The document listing, for each step, the check, method, frequency, who does it and the reaction plan
Data logger (weld monitor)
A device that records the current and voltage of each weld for later checking
External failure cost
The cost of a fault found by the customer after delivery
First-off
A full inspection of the first part after a set-up, before the run goes on
Hold point
A point in the work that may not be passed until the named person has checked and released it
Internal failure cost
The cost of faults found before delivery: rework, repair, scrap, lost time
Last-off
The last part of a run, checked and kept to prove the process was still right at the end
Non-conformance report (NCR)
The record of a non-conformance, its containment, cause, disposition and corrective action
Pareto chart
A bar chart ranking fault types from most to least common
Patrol (in-process) inspection
Checks made at set times at each work station during production
Poka-yoke (mistake-proofing)
Designing a jig or method so a mistake cannot be made, or is seen at once
Prevention cost
Money spent to stop faults happening: training, work instructions, jigs
Process audit
An audit that checks the line works to its procedures and records
Product audit
An audit that checks finished parts against the drawing
Reaction plan
What to do when a check fails, written in advance
Root cause
The underlying cause that, once removed, stops the fault coming back
Run chart
A measurement plotted in time order with a centre line
Tightened sampling
Checking more parts after a failure until results are good again
Traceability
Being able to tell from the records who made a part, when, from what, and how it was checked
Trial (set-up) piece
A part made to prove the set-up, then cut or tested and not sent out

c1.title: Roof trusses for a school in Linstead
c1.text: Nordia is the quality monitor on a line making 160 identical steel roof trusses for a new school block in Linstead, St Catherine. The control plan calls for a full first-off check, a patrol check of every 8th truss, and a control chart of the heel-joint fillet leg. The drawing asks for a 6 mm leg with a tolerance of 6–8 mm. Readings from earlier runs of this truss average 7.0 mm, with a standard deviation of 0.2 mm.

c2.title: Lack of fusion on a panel line in Portmore
c2.text: Damion monitors three manual MIG stations welding burglar-bar panels in Portmore, St Catherine. Last week's inspection found 80 faults: lack of fusion 46, porosity 12, spatter 9, undercut 8 and wrong size 5. Of the 46 lack-of-fusion faults, 34 came from Station 2. The settings log shows that on Tuesday the Station 2 welder turned the wire speed down from 9.0 to 7.0 m/min "to cut the spatter". The WPS range is 8.5–10.0 m/min.

c3.title: The monthly figures at a tank-stand shop in Mandeville
c3.text: Yanique writes the monthly quality report for a shop in Mandeville, Manchester, that makes steel water-tank stands. Last month there were 26 hours of rework at J$2 800 an hour, J$12 400 of rework consumables, J$9 600 of scrapped steel, and one site repair at a customer in Christiana that cost J$38 000 in travel and labour. The production manager is considering a new jig and a day of welder training, costing J$150 000 in all, which is expected to halve the rework and scrap.

c4.title: Balcony rails for galvanising in Savanna-la-Mar
c4.text: Garfield monitors the welding of 120 balcony railing panels in square hollow section for an apartment block in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. The panels will be hot-dip galvanised. The drawing shows two 10 mm vent and drain holes at each closed end of every hollow member. This week the welders started using a new anti-spatter spray from a different supplier; its label says it is silicone-based. The customer's specification asks for material certificates and a record of who welded each panel.

c5.title: A dropped gauge in May Pen
c5.text: Tavia is the day-shift quality monitor at a shop in May Pen, Clarendon, that makes steel frames for market stalls. At 10:00 a.m. she drops the station's fillet gauge set on the concrete floor; it looks undamaged, so she carries on with her patrol checks. In the afternoon she notices that the work instruction posted at Station 4 is Revision B, while the office copy is Revision C, issued last week with a new tack order.

questions.q: The first-off truss is 8 mm over its overall length tolerance, although its welds are good. What should happen?
o: Hold the run, fix the jig and check a new first-off
Start the run and check the second truss more closely
Start the run, as the welds on this truss are all good
Weld the batch, then trim each truss to length after
questions.why: A first-off proves the set-up before the run goes on. If it fails, the run does not start: the jig is corrected and another first-off is made and checked, so the fault is not copied into 160 trusses.

questions.q: How many patrol checks will the run of trusses need?
questions.why: One truss in every 8 is checked: 160 ÷ 8 = 20 patrol checks, as well as the first-off and last-off checks.

questions.q: Using the average ± 3 standard deviations, where should Nordia draw the control limits for the leg size?
o: At 6.0 mm and 8.0 mm
At 6.6 mm and 7.4 mm
At 6.8 mm and 7.2 mm
At 6.4 mm and 7.6 mm
questions.why: 3 × 0.2 = 0.6 mm, so the limits are 7.0 − 0.6 = 6.4 mm and 7.0 + 0.6 = 7.6 mm. Control limits come from the process data; 6–8 mm is the drawing's tolerance, a different thing.

questions.q: Nordia compares the 6.4–7.6 mm spread of the process with the 6–8 mm tolerance. What does this show?
o: It fits with room to spare if kept centred
It cannot meet the tolerance, so check every truss
The drawing tolerance should be tightened to match
The spread is too wide, so the sampling must stop
questions.why: The process spread is 1.2 mm inside a 2 mm tolerance (Cp ≈ 1.7), so it is capable as long as it stays centred. The chart is still kept, because drift can use up that margin.

questions.q: What share of last week's faults was lack of fusion?
o: About 46%
About 43%
About 58%
About 74%
questions.why: Share = 46 ÷ 80 × 100 = 57.5%, about 58%. The other figures come from mixing up the numbers: 34 ÷ 80 is about 43%, and 34 ÷ 46 is about 74%.

questions.q: What does the split of lack-of-fusion faults by station suggest?
o: A batch of faulty wire used by all three of the stations
A cause at Station 2: its settings, machine or method
Normal variation, as every station had some faults
The inspector checking Station 2 is stricter than the rest
questions.why: When one station produces most of one fault, the cause is likely to be something only that station shares: its settings, machine, welder or method. A wire batch used everywhere would show up at all three stations.

questions.q: What was wrong with the Station 2 welder's change of wire speed?
o: It put the setting outside the WPS range without approval
Nothing: lowering the wire speed was a sensible fix for spatter
It should have been written in the log at the end of the week
Only voltage is fixed by a WPS; wire speed may be changed
questions.why: 7.0 m/min is below the WPS range of 8.5–10.0 m/min. Less wire speed means less current and colder welds, which explains the lack of fusion; every panel welded since Tuesday is suspect.

questions.q: Station 2 has been reset to the WPS. How should Damion show the fix has worked?
o: Close the problem, since the setting is now right
Have the welder sign that he will not change it
Sample Station 2 more often and watch the data
Look at Station 2 again at the next monthly audit
questions.why: A fix is proved by results: tightened sampling for a time and the fault figures falling and staying down. Only then is the problem closed and the work instruction or training updated.

questions.q: What was last month's internal failure cost?
questions.why: Internal failures are found before delivery: 26 × J$2 800 = J$72 800, plus J$12 400 consumables and J$9 600 scrap, totals J$94 800. The J$38 000 site repair is an external failure cost.

questions.q: If the jig and training halve the rework and scrap, about how long will the J$150 000 take to pay back?
o: About 1 month
About 3 months
About 6 months
About 16 months
questions.why: Half of J$94 800 is J$47 400 saved each month, and J$150 000 ÷ J$47 400 ≈ 3.2 months. Any fall in site repairs would make the payback even quicker.

questions.q: To save money, the manager suggests dropping the patrol checks. Which costs are most likely to rise?
o: Prevention costs, such as welder training and new jigs
Appraisal costs, such as gauges and the inspectors' time
Failure costs, especially faults reaching customers
None, as the welders will simply take more care
questions.why: Patrol checks are an appraisal cost, so dropping them saves a little. But drift then goes unnoticed, so more faults are found late or by customers, and external failures are the most expensive of all.

questions.q: A patrol check finds several panels welded without their vent and drain holes. What should Garfield do?
o: Pass them: the galvaniser can drill any holes needed
Pass them, as the holes only affect the inside coating
Seal every end fully with weld so no zinc gets inside
Hold them: sealed sections can burst in the zinc
questions.why: Air and moisture trapped in a sealed section expand violently in molten zinc at about 450 °C, and zinc cannot drain in and out to coat the inside. The panels are held and the holes made before they leave.

questions.q: What should be done about the new silicone-based anti-spatter spray?
o: Stop it until approved; zinc will not stick to silicone
Allow it, as anti-spatter spray never affects the coating
Allow it, as the galvaniser's acid cleaning removes residues
Use more of it, so the spatter lifts off the panels more easily
questions.why: Silicone is not removed by the galvaniser's normal cleaning, so it leaves bare, uncoated patches. A new consumable is a change: it is checked and approved before use, and here the galvaniser should be asked.

questions.q: How can Garfield show the customer that the steel is the grade on the drawing?
o: Ask the delivery driver to sign that the steel is the right grade
Rely on the colour code painted on the ends of the lengths
Weigh the steel and compare the weight with the order
Match the steel's heat numbers to its mill certificates
questions.why: Each length is marked with a heat number that matches its mill (material) certificate. Matching and filing them, with a record of who welded each panel, gives the traceability the specification asks for.

questions.q: What should Tavia have done after dropping the gauge set?
o: Kept using it, as it showed no sign of damage
Averaged its readings with another inspector's
Checked it against a reference before reuse
Used it only on welds that looked borderline
questions.why: A dropped gauge can be knocked out of true without any visible mark. It is checked against a known reference before further use, and every reading taken with it since the drop is in doubt.

questions.q: What should be done about the Revision B work instruction at Station 4?
o: Leave it up for now, as the welders know Revision B well
Put Revision C up beside it, so the welders can choose one
Wait for the next process audit to sort out the documents
Put up Revision C, brief the welders and check the frames
questions.why: Only the current revision may be at the station. Remove the old copy, brief the welders on the new tack order, and check the frames made to Revision B since it was issued.

questions.q: A team writes a problem at the head of a diagram, with branches for people, machines, methods, materials, measurement and environment. What tool is this?
o: A Pareto chart of the fault types found
A fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram
A control chart with its centre line
A process flow chart of the whole line
questions.why: A fishbone diagram lists possible causes of one problem under the 6 Ms. The team then checks the likely causes against the data or with a trial.

questions.q: Porosity at a station was traced back: poor gas cover, then low flow at the nozzle, then a knocked regulator, then a cylinder trolley parked where the forklift turns. What is the root cause to fix?
o: Poor gas cover over the weld pool
Low gas flow at the gun nozzle
No safe, marked place for the cylinder
The regulator that was knocked out of setting
questions.why: Asking "why?" until a removable cause is reached leads to the cylinder's position. Resetting the regulator alone would let the same accident happen again; a marked cylinder bay stops it.

questions.q: A batch of frames has stiffener fillets 1 mm under size. The production manager wants to send them as they are. What is needed?
o: The production manager's spoken agreement
Written approval from the designer or customer
Nothing, since the stiffener is not critical
A note about it on the delivery docket for the customer
questions.why: Accepting a non-conforming part as it is (a concession) needs the written approval of whoever owns the design, usually the designer or customer. Without it, the parts are repaired or rejected.

questions.q: The inspection and test plan shows a hold point for the customer's inspector at the first-off. The inspector is running late. What should the team do?
o: Wait: the run cannot pass a hold point until released
Start the run, and show the first-off to the inspector later
Carry on, because a hold point is only a piece of advice
Weld and ship the first-off now, then carry on with the run
questions.why: At a hold point, work stops until the named person has checked and released it, or has waived it in writing. A witness point is different: work may continue if the inspector does not come.
